# Draft:Republican makeup

Republican makeup, also MAGA makeup, MAGA beauty or conservative girl makeup, is a pejorative term used by American progressives for the way women who support or work for Donald Trump apparently prefer to apply their cosmetics. It is depicted as wearing makeup, such as eyeliner, mascara, rouge and foundation, so heavily as to make its use obvious. Republican Congresswomen such as Nancy Mace and women working in the second Trump administration like Kristi Noem, and several Fox News commentators, have been cited as examples.
Suzanne Lambert, a comedian on TikTok, is credited with popularizing the concept through a video she made shortly after Trump's victory in the November 2024 presidential election. After noticing it on women who indicated they supported Trump when leaving comments on her previous videos, she attempted to replicate the style with her own makeup. She told viewers the goal was a "dusty, drained" look. Later, other Internet personalities with progressive political leanings who focused on online beauty advice made their own videos with their take on the look. Trump's press secretary Karoline Leavitt posted a video of her makeup routine on social media that showed her using some of the techniques Lambert had mocked.
Some Republican women online have responded, criticizing Lambert and those who ridiculed the style as being hypocritical for allegedly otherwise preaching tolerance of others' choices. Others have countered by mocking "liberal makeup", focusing on the blue-dyed hair of Democratic congresswoman Rosa DeLauro. There have also been criticisms from the left. Academics and fashion writers have also written critiques, observing that the Republican makeup look embodies an exaggerated aesthetic of gender performance that evokes drag queens, suggests that the superficial is the only important aspect of political policies, and marks the merger of political and celebrity culture.
Background
Texas makeup artist Stephanie Louise got the assignment to make up Lara Trump, the then-former president's daughter-in-law, for her speaking slot at the 2024 Republican National Convention. In an Instagram video, she detailed the various products she used and her techniques: blending three different shades of eye shadow along with eyeliner and false lashes to create "a respectful eye" and eschewing contouring. The look may have helped Trump get her own show on Fox News.
After the elections, Washington-based comedian and influencer Suzanne Lambert, who had supported Kamala Harris and other Democratic candidates in the elections, noticed that many of the women attacking her and supporting Republicans and President-elect Donald Trump in comments on her TikTok videos seemed to wear their makeup in the same distinctive style. As a self-described "Regina George liberal", who advocates for Democrats and political progressives to respond to Republican attacks in kind, she decided to devote a video to trying to reproduce that style.
Technique
Lambert posted her video, "Doing my makeup like the gorg maga girlies in my comments", to her TikTok feed on November 16. She styled it as an online makeup tutorial, looking at the camera from across a table, a headband holding back her hair as she applied makeup to her face, wearing a Waffle House sweatshirt and addressing viewers as "we" while Gretchen Wilson's "Redneck Girl" plays softly in the background. After briefly explaining her inspiration for the video, she begins.
The first step involves foregoing the usual application of moisturizer or primer. "We really want our makeup to cling to any dry spots and accentuate any texture we might have," Lambert said. After that came foundation that did not match the wearer's skin tone, usually too dark. "It's giving drained, it's giving dusty", she comments. "We want to make sure that it doesn't look like we've ever used moisturizer once in our life." Instead of using a brush to spread the foundation around and blend it with the face's natural tones, Lambert uses her fingers to ensure a streaky appearance. She also put extra tanner on her hands to ensure tones that do not match.
Concealer came next, under the eyes. In keeping with the deliberately mismatched foundation, Lambert advises the use of a tone several shades lighter than the makeup's base. "Make sure you really get it into the crease so it settles under the fine lines. That's really important." Again she reminded viewers to rub it in instead of patting it. "Instead of blending it out to make it look smooth, we're just kind of smearing it to other parts." Eyebrow pencil should be applied liberally to give a blocky look which she likened to that produced by an online photo filter, "but in real life and not totally matching." She uses, and recommends, Anastasia Brow Whiz, applied as if in the dark to keep the line from being too straight. Contouring and bronzer are to be avoided. "We are going for matte and flat", Lambert says, as she indicates some areas she will leave unblended, "just to make it look more authentic."
Lambert recommends that, again, when rouge in Republican makeup, that a tone at odds with the viewer's natural tones be chosen. She applies low on her face, to avoid an "uplifted, Bella Hadid effect." Instead, the goal is to "make it look like everything is drooping." This brought her to the eyes, which she described as her favorite part of this look. By starting with the lightest possible eye shadow, applied to the whole upper eyelid, it was possible to make the eyes appear smaller, Lambert showed. The effect is enhanced with "an old-fashioned smoky eye."
Heavy black eyeliner, applied to both the top and bottom, finishes the eyes, Lambert explains. "It doesn't matter if it's straight, as long as it's thick ... Don't forget that when you are doing the bottom, you don't want to miss the waterline." She uses a downward motion with the brush to give what she describes as that "'is she awake'? effect." Lastly she uses the driest mascara she can find on her eyelashes, making sure to leave visible clumps. "Get a little on the eyelids too, and don't clean it up."
Lipstick to complete the look should be a very tame skin tone, in keeping with the overall "matte and flat" theme, without any lip liner, Lambert counseled. The wearer should remember to tuck her top lip under when smiling. At the end, Lambert added a brightly lit still photo of herself with a flower band digitally added around her head. "Let me know how I did", she asks.
The video got 4.7 million views and many favorable comments. In an interview with Glamour two months later, after the media began reporting on the trend, Lambert elaborated. If the women making themselves up this way used any primer, she said, "it's likely a silicone-based primer that does not go with their water-based foundation. The foundation never matches their undertones. They love a golden undertone when a lot of them should be wearing a cool tone like me." That was offset by an apparently sunburned neck and chest since it did not seem to Lambert that Republican women ever used sunscreen. The goal of the eye makeup in the style should be "that raccoon-eye look."
Other interpretations
Other Internet personalities offered their takes on the style. One said afterwards she was glad she was Canadian. YouTuber Frederic Chen created a more exaggerated version, with commentary more overtly political, citing South Carolina Representative Nancy Mace as an inspiration despite calling her "a hot piece of garbage", and the style as making women wearing it look like zombies. He also made broader commentary about the transphobia among the MAGA base, linking it to aspects of the style:
The New York Times observed that the look is usually sartorially complemented by form-fitting clothing and conspicuous cross necklaces.
Karoline Leavitt video
In a resurfaced video reel of her makeup routine Karoline Leavitt, Trump's press secretary, had posted to her Instagram feed some time before taking the position, she appeared to lend Lambert's take on Republican makeup credibility by using some of the same techniques. She purposely used foundation darker than her skin tone, which Luna Viola, a Los Angeles makeup artist, told fashion website The List is a common error when trying to add dimension. Leavitt also chose an overly dark contour stick, compounding the problem. She put it on "slightly too low, dragging the cheekbones down and resulting in an unnatural placement", Viola says. The video also showed Leavitt using her fingertips to spread her makeup around, as Lambert had speculated would be done. Luna cautioned against this not only for the poor blending but for sanitary reasons.
Some commenters on the video in early 2025 noted the unintentional confirmation of Lambert's take, with one calling Leavitt's video "beyond hilarious." The original video is no longer available, but some excerpts have been used in online commentary.
Reaction
By the time Trump was inaugurated, Lambert's video had reached over 6 million views, and gained her followers including Jen Psaki, the former Joe Biden press secretary and now MSNBC host, and Jonathan Van Ness of Queer Eye for the Straight Guy. The media began to take notice, with The Washington Post running a story on the video as exemplifying Lambert's advocacy of "Regina George liberalism", named after the Mean Girls character—"when they go low we go mean".
